## Before we begin {.question-slide}

::: {.big-question}
What does a machine see when it reads this sentence?
:::

::: {.sentence}
“NLP isn't just words 🤔”
:::

::: {.fragment .answer}
Not words. Not meaning. **Numbers.**
:::

## Tokenization, in one line

::: {.definition}
**Tokenization** segments text into the units a model will process.
:::

::: {.token-demo}
<span class="raw">NLP is fascinating!</span>
<span class="down">↓</span>
<span class="token t1">NLP</span><span class="token t2">is</span><span class="token t3">fascinating</span><span class="token t4">!</span>
:::

:::: {.two-col .terms}
::: {}
**Token**

One occurrence in an input
:::
::: {}
**Vocabulary**

All distinct units the model knows
:::
::::

## The choice that changes everything

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .chars}
### Characters

`t · o · k · e · n`

Small vocabulary  
Long sequences
:::
::: {.card .words}
### Words

`tokenization`

Short sequences  
Huge vocabulary
:::
::: {.card .subwords}
### Subwords

`token · ization`

The modern compromise
:::
::::

# Characters {.section-slide}

## Character-level: the superpower

::: {.character-line}
<span>r</span><span>e</span><span>t</span><span>o</span><span>k</span><span>e</span><span>n</span><span>i</span><span>z</span><span>a</span><span>t</span><span>i</span><span>o</span><span>n</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .superpower}
✓ Tiny vocabulary &nbsp;&nbsp; ✓ Can spell any new word &nbsp;&nbsp; ✓ No unknown words
:::

## …and the price

:::: {.sequence-compare}
::: {}
**Words** · 4 positions

<span class="token word">Tokenization</span> <span class="token word">helps</span> <span class="token word">language</span> <span class="token word">models</span>
:::
::: {.fragment}
**Characters** · 41 positions

<span class="tiny-sequence">T o k e n i z a t i o n · h e l p s · l a n g u a g e · m o d e l s</span>
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
Meaning is spread over many positions; computation grows with sequence length.
:::

# Words {.section-slide}

## Word-level feels natural

::: {.token-demo .compact}
<span class="raw">Tokenization is useful.</span>
<span class="down">↓</span>
<span class="token t1">Tokenization</span><span class="token t2">is</span><span class="token t3">useful</span><span class="token t4">.</span>
:::

::: {.superpower}
✓ Intuitive units &nbsp;&nbsp; ✓ Short sequences &nbsp;&nbsp; ✓ Meaningful pieces
:::

## Language refuses to stay in a list

::: {.word-family}
<span class="known">train ✓</span>
<span class="known">trained ✓</span>
<span class="unknown fragment">retrained ?</span>
<span class="unknown fragment">retraining ?</span>
<span class="unknown fragment">trainability ?</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .unk-box}
`retraining` → **`<UNK>`**

`hyperparameterization` → **`<UNK>`**
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
Names, inflections, technical terms, typos, and hashtags never stop arriving.
:::

## The impossible triangle

::: {.triangle-wrap}
<div class="triangle"></div>
<div class="tri-label top">Small vocabulary</div>
<div class="tri-label left">Short sequences</div>
<div class="tri-label right">New-word coverage</div>
<div class="tri-center">Choose<br/>two?</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
Characters deliver vocabulary + coverage. Words deliver short sequences. Ask what could sit between them. 2 minutes.
:::

# Subwords {.section-slide}

## The useful middle ground

::: {.split-examples}
`the` → <span class="token t2">the</span>

`tokenization` → <span class="token t1">token</span><span class="token t3">ization</span>

`unhappiness` → <span class="token t4">un</span><span class="token t2">happi</span><span class="token t1">ness</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Keep frequent forms whole. Split rare forms into reusable pieces.
:::

## BPE: learn pieces from repetition

::: {.bpe}
<div><strong>Start</strong> &nbsp; l · o · w · e · r</div>
<div class="fragment"><strong>Merge</strong> &nbsp; <mark>lo</mark> · w · e · r</div>
<div class="fragment"><strong>Merge</strong> &nbsp; <mark>low</mark> · e · r</div>
<div class="fragment"><strong>Merge</strong> &nbsp; <mark>low</mark> · <mark>er</mark></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .algorithm}
Count adjacent pairs → merge the frequent pair → repeat
:::

<div class="citation">Simplified intuition for byte-pair encoding [@sennrich2016subword].</div>

## Same idea, different recipes

| Family | Core intuition | Seen in |
|---|---|---|
| **BPE** | Merge frequent neighbors | GPT-style models |
| **WordPiece** | Add pieces that improve likelihood | BERT |
| **Unigram** | Remove pieces the model needs least | SentencePiece models |
| **Byte-level** | Start from bytes: nothing is unknown | GPT-2 / RoBERTa |

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The tokenizer and its vocabulary **belong to the model**.
:::

<div class="citation">[@schuster2012wordpiece; @kudo2018subwordregularization; @kudo2018sentencepiece; @wang2019bytelevel]</div>

# Try it {.section-slide}

## A tiny regex tokenizer

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3|5-6"}
import re

pattern = r"\b\w+(?:['’]\w+)?\b|[^\w\s]"

text = "NLP isn't just words—it includes punctuation!"
re.findall(pattern, text)
```

::: {.fragment .code-output}
`['NLP', "isn't", 'just', 'words', '—', 'it', 'includes', 'punctuation', '!']`
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Regex is excellent when **you can state the rules**. It is not a universal tokenizer.
:::

## Let a language library handle the rules

```python
import spacy

nlp = spacy.blank("en")
text = "Don't email support@example.com—visit example.com."

[token.text for token in nlp(text)]
```

::: {.fragment .code-output}
`['Do', "n't", 'email', 'support@example.com', '—', 'visit', 'example.com', '.']`
:::

<div class="citation">spaCy uses general rules plus language-specific exceptions [@spacy2026tokenization].</div>

## Ask the model's own tokenizer

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
tok.tokenize("Tokenizers tokenize unseen tokenization!")
```

::: {.fragment .code-output}
`['token', '##izer', '##s', 'token', '##ize', 'unseen', 'token', '##ization', '!']`
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
`##` means “continue the current word” in this WordPiece vocabulary.
:::

## Checkpoint {.question-slide}

::: {.big-question}
Why are subwords the modern default?
:::

:::: {.fragment .three-col .compact-cards}
::: {.mini-card}
**Coverage**

Rare words can be decomposed
:::
::: {.mini-card}
**Efficiency**

Sequences stay manageable
:::
::: {.mini-card}
**Reuse**

Pieces recur across words
:::
::::

# From IDs to meaning {.section-slide}

## Token IDs are addresses—not meaning

::: {.id-row}
<div><span class="token t1">king</span><strong>→ 547</strong></div>
<div><span class="token t2">queen</span><strong>→ 2938</strong></div>
<div><span class="token t3">banana</span><strong>→ 89</strong></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .wrong-math}
Is `queen > king`? &nbsp; Is `king ≈ banana`?
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
The numbers only identify rows in a table. Their magnitude is arbitrary.
:::

## One-hot vectors keep identity…

::: {.one-hot-grid}
<div><strong>king</strong><code>[0, 1, 0, 0, 0]</code></div>
<div><strong>queen</strong><code>[0, 0, 0, 1, 0]</code></div>
<div><strong>banana</strong><code>[1, 0, 0, 0, 0]</code></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .big-equation}
distance(king, queen) = distance(king, banana)
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
…but says that every different word is equally unrelated.
:::

## Embeddings give words coordinates

:::: {.embedding-layout}
::: {.embedding-vector}
**queen**

`[0.18, −0.71, 0.42, …]`

50–300 learned dimensions
:::
::: {.semantic-map}
<span class="point royal king">king</span>
<span class="point royal queen">queen</span>
<span class="point human man">man</span>
<span class="point human woman">woman</span>
<span class="point fruit apple">apple</span>
<span class="point fruit banana">banana</span>
<span class="axis x">dimension ? →</span>
<span class="axis y">dimension ? →</span>
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Words used in similar contexts learn nearby positions.
:::

## Similarity becomes geometry

::: {.cosine-visual}
<div class="origin"></div>
<div class="vector v1"><span>king</span></div>
<div class="vector v2"><span>queen</span></div>
<div class="vector v3"><span>banana</span></div>
:::

::: {.cosine-formula}
$$\cos(\theta)=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Small angle → similar direction → often similar meaning or usage.
:::

## The famous analogy

::: {.analogy}
<span class="token t1">king</span>
<span class="operator">−</span>
<span class="token t3">man</span>
<span class="operator">+</span>
<span class="token t2">woman</span>
<span class="operator">≈</span>
<span class="token t4">queen</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .analogy-caption}
The vector from **man → woman** resembles the vector from **king → queen**.
:::

::: {.fragment .warning}
Powerful illustration—not a law of language. Embeddings also inherit stereotypes and biases from their data.
:::

## Ask a pretrained embedding

```python
import gensim.downloader as api

wv = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")

wv.most_similar("language", topn=5)
wv.most_similar(positive=["king", "woman"],
                negative=["man"], topn=3)
```

::: {.fragment .code-output}
`language → languages, spoken, english, dialect, word`

`king − man + woman → queen, monarch, throne`
:::

<div class="citation">GloVe vectors accessed through Gensim KeyedVectors [@rehurek2026keyedvectors]. Exact neighbors can vary by model.</div>

## What a 100-D space looks like in 2-D

::: {.semantic-map .large-map}
<span class="cluster-label royalty-label">royalty</span>
<span class="point royal king">king</span>
<span class="point royal queen">queen</span>
<span class="point royal prince">prince</span>
<span class="point human man">man</span>
<span class="point human woman">woman</span>
<span class="cluster-label people-label">people</span>
<span class="point fruit apple">apple</span>
<span class="point fruit banana">banana</span>
<span class="point fruit orange">orange</span>
<span class="cluster-label fruit-label">fruit</span>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
PCA compresses the view for us; the model still uses the full vector.
:::

:::

:::

→

Tokenization decides the **pieces**.  
Embeddings give those pieces a **geometry**.
